blocks.h2: Does Your Basement Need an Overhead Sewer System?
blocks.intro: There are several signs your basement needs an overhead sewer system. Some are subtle. Others aren't. Here's what to look for, from mild to severe:

tiles.h3: Water at the Floor Drain When It Rains Hard
tiles.body: A little backup at the floor drain during heavy rain, gone by morning. Easy to ignore. It's usually the first sign your sewer connection can't keep up.
The line gets [rodded](/highland-park/sewer-rodding), it clears, and a few weeks later the backup returns. That's not a clogging problem anymore. It's a sign the connection itself is the limit.

tiles.h3: A Backup That's Already Caused Damage
tiles.body: Sewage in a finished basement. Ruined flooring, drywall, belongings. At this point, another temporary fix isn't worth the risk of round two.

blocks.h2: How an Overhead Sewer System Works
blocks.body: Every drain below the street sewer's flow line, like your floor drain, a basement bathroom, or a laundry line, normally relies on gravity to reach the sewer. An overhead sewer system reroutes those drains into a sump pit instead. An [ejector pump](/highland-park/ejector-pump) lifts that wastewater up to a line above flood level, where a check valve keeps it from flowing back down. From there, gravity carries it the rest of the way to the street sewer, the same as every drain upstairs.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewers and Highland Park Basements
blocks.intro: The City of Highland Park's own flood tips name overhead sewer systems as one way to help prevent sewer backups, along with backflow preventers and sump pumps with battery backups.

items.h3: Older Homes Built on Straight Gravity
items.body: The median Highland Park home was built in 1963, and plenty of older homes run on a straight gravity connection with no overhead system at all. Finished basements in those homes have the most to lose.

Highland Park runs separate sanitary and storm sewers, so a wet basement here isn't always a sewer backup. Groundwater calls for a [sump pump](/highland-park/sump-pumps), a blocked private line calls for [rodding](/highland-park/sewer-rodding), and a low connection that can't keep up calls for an overhead system. We'll tell you which one you're dealing with.
The homeowner owns and maintains the private sewer line from the house to the city main. We check that line on camera before recommending a conversion, so you're not paying to fix the wrong problem.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewer vs. Sump Pump vs. Backwater Valve
blocks.intro: A sump pump, a backwater valve, and an overhead sewer system each solve a different basement water problem, and only one of them fixes a sewer connection that's reached its limit.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewer Questions From Highland Park Homeowners

items.q: How do I know if I need an overhead sewer system?
items.preview: Start with how often it happens. A backup that returns after rodding is a strong sign.
items.answer: Start with how often it happens and how bad it's gotten. An occasional backup at the floor drain during heavy rain is an early sign. If you've had the line rodded and the backup keeps coming back, that's a sign the connection itself can't keep up. If it's already caused real damage, that's the clearest sign of all.

items.q: Is an overhead sewer required in Highland Park?
items.preview: It depends on the property and the project. We check what applies during the assessment.
items.answer: Some jurisdictions require an overhead sewer system in specific situations, but there's no single blanket rule across every city we serve. We'll check what applies to your property and your plans, like finishing a basement, during the assessment.

items.q: Do I need an overhead sewer or a sump pump?
items.preview: They solve different problems: groundwater versus sewer backup. We help you figure out which you have.
items.answer: They solve different problems. A sump pump handles groundwater coming through the foundation. An overhead sewer system stops sewage from backing up through basement drains. Highland Park runs separate storm and sanitary sewers, so it's worth pinning down which water you're seeing before choosing a fix.

items.q: How long does overhead sewer installation take?
items.preview: Most installations take 2 to 5 days, depending on your home's layout.
items.answer: Most overhead sewer installations take 2 to 5 days, depending on your home's layout and how the connection needs to be routed.

items.q: How much does an overhead sewer system cost?
items.preview: Cost depends on your home's layout and depth. You get a flat rate before any work begins.
items.answer: Cost depends on a few things specific to your home: how deep the connection needs to go, your home's layout, whether an ejector pit is already in place or needs to be added, and how easy the work area is to access. We'll walk through all of that with you and give you a flat rate before any work begins.
